title: Nine Stories
author: J.D. Salinger
thoughts: I started this year reading all of Salinger’s short stories, in an attempt to stitch together the story of the Glass family. It was a task much simpler than I thought it would be, and I loved doing it! If every Glass family story was complied into one novel, it would be among my favorites. Bananafish and For Esme are still my favorites in this collection, however I learned to love the other’s much more than I used to. Truly what I believe to be among the best examples of what great writing looks like.

title: Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction
author: J.D. Salinger
thoughts: What I believed would be at the tail end of my favorite Glass family stories ended up being at the top of said list. Raise High the Roof Beam, has the depth and plot to be a standalone story, but when read along with the others it adds so much depth to the family members. I adore how much you can tell Buddy cares for his older brother in this story, my god it’s so heartwarming and realistic. Seymour is less of a standalone, with content similar to Franny and Zooey. Prose wise, I do not get how Salinger does it, it is written so realistically it feels like there are no characters and you are hearing him candidly speak. This story also has one of the best, probably my favorite, lines in all of literature!

title: The Buried Giant
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
thoughts: I really enjoyed this book, it was a fun light-fantasy read with a strong core. Like most Ishiguro books, the ending is where everything in the book coalesces and what he was trying to get across comes out. The heart of this novel, what Ishiguro was trying to say, was important and made me think about it for a while afterwards. While the story was fun, I think it would have been an amazing book if the story wasn’t so conventional, like its a good genre read, but the story was not doing anything incredibly different or noteworthy.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway
thoughts: I truly believe it is the bell curve once again, where because it is a simple but well written story, it will be liked by very novice readers (left side of the curve), but also people who think so much of literature that they end up wrapping around and their opinions become like, its the simple stories that are the best (right side). Just did not do much, and I get it, this would be meaningful to me if I had lived a whole life and I was like god damn 90 years old. I think you just need to have read all of Hemingway to enjoy this one, as like a final dessert.

title: The Unconsoled
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
thoughts: I am sorry but this novel felt like the try not the laugh equivalent for your literary patience. Ishiguro, I get what we were trying to do, and I think you aced exactly that, which was how to write dream-like narratives or disillusioned states, but 500+ pages to do that and not <100? LMFAO.

title: The Dispossessed
author: Ursula K. LeGuin
thoughts: Before reading Ursula K. LeGuin, you don’t think about how there is basically a single understanding of what science fiction is. Then you read her literature and you realize that she fundamentally looks at science fiction differently. Like she derived it from an entirely unique set of base principles. To write a novel where what is alien to us is not in culture or looks or language, but in politics and relationships is so very interesting and impressive!

title: The Last Samurai
author: Helen DeWitt
thoughts: A post-modern novel about a precocious child’s obsession with literature, Kurosawa and the Japanese language? Yeah, I wear my biases on my sleeve! I really liked this book, it was fun, sweet at times, and incredibly smart. This book made me really believe that Helen DeWitt is a genius, like with all respect and genuine praise, I do not think you can be neurotypical and write a novel this grand.

title: The Left Hand of Darkness
author: Ursula K. LeGuin
thoughts: What was said in my The Dispossessed review spans to this one as well. Again, she recontextualizes what is considered alien to us, in-part by seeing us as the alien, this time through sex and biology which intersects very realistically with politics. I think about the fictional process of kemmer which is a focus in this novel, and how interesting it is to think about what really is normal and how subjective that is.

title: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay
author: Michael Chabon
thoughts: If you read the blurb of what this novel is about and do not think it's already the coolest piece of media ever, click out. What a lovely and fun and monumental read. Every character is written with such depth and care. It’s treats itself serious at times but at others it can be read similarly to a comic book. I usually despise the depiction of artists in media but Chabon writes it with such understanding. Greatness!

title: This is for Everyone
author: Tim Berners Lee
thoughts: Half memoir, half history lesson, and half manifesto, this book is really something great. It follows Tim Berners Lee throughout his life, up to when he created the WWW, and straight through it to today. It’s so interesting to hear about the thought process behind some of the most invisible but important things I take for granted. I find him deeply admirable for his choices and beliefs when it comes to the free internet and his views on education. I must-read for anyone who cares for the internet.

title: The Crying of Lot 49
author: Thomas Pynchon
thoughts: This was me trying to start reading Pynchon, and I know I am going to regret this review later on in life. But I just did not really like the novel, thank god it was so short. The prose is incredibly dense, I think I read this online and its so true, but its like trying to swallow a baseball. Theres just so much in each sentence, it's impressive, but I did not care for the story or characters.

title: Underworld
author: Don DeLillo
thoughts: Any other writer would have told the same story in a 180 page text, however Don DeLillo manages to miraculously cross the 800 page line. Like most post-modern literature, I loved the structure, which slows you at times but allows the novel to feel much larger than it is. The baseball mcguffin should have had more emphasis, it did at times but fell through at others. Overall good, but dragged on for me, I enjoyed it more than White Noise honestly.

title: Pachinko
author: Min Jin Lee
thoughts: A wide account of Japan and Korea during the 20th century through a multi-generational narrative structure, which reminded me at times of Steinbeck’s East of Eden. It was a quick read but very enjoyable. While the first generation was very well written, the novel started the lose me at the seemingly exponential speed at which it was progressing. Some of the later characters were hard to understand deeper than a surface level, which led me to not feel much of an impact at important moments. This novel could have easily been 800+ pages and I would not have questioned its length at all, I would have welcomed it.

title: The Cowshed
author: Ji Xianlin
thoughts: A very enlightening first-person account for anyone who is interested in an academic’s side of China's cultural revolution. It is a great read but I would treat it more like a supplemental material than what I would recommend to be a start or cover-all for learning about the cultural revolution. I am being harsh, it was an important and great read!

title: When We Cease to Understand the World
author: Benjamin Labatut
thoughts: I found this book brilliant, both in content and prose. It is self-contained and feels grand due to the weight of the accounts depicted. While reading, I questioned the frequency and extent of fiction’s inclusion. But when you take the entire novel as a whole, I find it reflects the core of what Labatut is trying to get at with these stories, the heart of the heart if you will.

title: Invisible Cities
author: Italo Calvino
thoughts: I just did not really enjoy this book. It felt as if I was reading a very well written writing excercise. Starting to think I have an aversion to small novels.
